newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong Varitronix tailors LCDs to taste.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong Varitronix tailors LCDs to taste.

text.p: Varitronix makes faces for machines to display what they are doing, sensing, feeling.
The Hong Kong company manufactures liquid crystal displays (LCDs), the flat indicator panels that show up on everything from calculators at the low end to laptop computers at the high.

The company's niche is in the middle. While LCDs on both the low and high ends are commodities churned out in automated factories with razor-thin margins, Varitronix makes displays customised to meet the needs of specific products.

Watch faces and computer screens all show basically the same information, but displays on each model of cellular phone or medical diagnostic unit are unique to that product, explained York Liao, managing director and head of research at Varitronix.
"Even rice cookers, the newest generation all have displays. Some cook congee (gruel), others can't, so their displays have to be different," Liao told Reuters in an interview.
Servicing this need to be different is the niche Varitronix occupies, and it is a growing as machines become ever more complex.
"Air conditioner remote controllers now have displays because you have to control more and more things," Liao said. "The display becomes a necessity to tell you what you're doing."
Varitronix, founded in 1978, has plants at two sites in south China and a factory in Malaysia. Development, engineering and testing is conducted in Hong Kong.

Customising LCDs involves more than just making it display what the buyer wants. Varitronix tries to get involved early in the product development of its customers so that it knows not only what the LCD has to display but how it fits in the product.
"When you sold a display in the past (for) a watch or a calculator or whatever, it wasn't a big challenge at all, you just drop it in and it will work.

"Now you can't do that. In a cellular phone, you can't just drop it in because your phone is very complicated already, it doesn't allow much room and you have to display a fairly complicated message," Liao explained.
A Varitronix LCD will be custom engineered so it can just be dropped in, he said. Customisation, however, was not enough to keep Varitronix ahead of the competition.
Liao said the company was moving up the ladder by offering innovations such as LCDs with drivers incorporated, eliminating the need for a separate chip board and saving space and power.

It also recently developed a colour LCD that does not require a colour filter. While it only shows three colours, that still allows it to display much more information than conventional monochrome LCDs.
As one of the few Hong Kong industrial companies with proprietary technology and a solid niche, Varitronix is a darling of international investors.
The company stumbled in its latest half-year results due to delays in opening its newest plant in China, resulting in flat earnings. But analysts were unconcerned.
"They were below expectation but not negative," said Morris MacLeod of ING Barings. "The underlying business is going well, and new capacity coming on line will benefit the second half."
Liao said the company was confident of everything under its control in the second half, although market conditions of course were unpredictable. He was also confident about the long term.

"A display is the most visible component in any product, so if there's a design you want in the display to distinguish your product, you have to tool that display specially. Even when you buy a calculator you look at the numbers, not the on-off switch.
"That's why there will not be a day when displays are all automated and produced en masse," he said. "It's like suits, there are garment factories but there will always be tailors."
